prompt: Where is almost all of the DNA in an animal cell found?

options.text: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Vacuole
Cell wall

feedback.b: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
feedback.c: Vacuoles store substances. Animal cells have only small ones, if any.
feedback.d: Animal cells don't have a cell wall.

hints: Which part of the cell controls the cell's activities?
solution: Almost all of a cell's DNA is in the **nucleus**, packed into chromosomes. That's why the nucleus controls the cell.

prompt: What is the name for a section of DNA that carries the instructions for making one protein?
hints: Each chromosome carries hundreds or thousands of these.
solution: A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for one protein.

prompt: How many chromosomes are there in a normal human body cell?
hints: Chromosomes come in pairs. One of each pair came from your mother and the other from your father.
solution: A human body cell has **46** chromosomes, in 23 pairs.

prompt: Put these in order from **smallest** to **largest**.
hints: A gene is a short section of a chromosome.
solution: Gene → chromosome → nucleus → cell. A gene is part of a chromosome, the chromosomes are inside the nucleus, and the nucleus is inside the cell.

prompt: Match each type of protein to its job.

right.text: Speeds up chemical reactions, such as digesting food
A chemical messenger carried in the blood
Builds body parts such as hair, nails and skin

hints: Amylase is found in saliva and helps break down starch.
solution: Enzymes speed up reactions. Hormones are chemical messengers. Antibodies help fight germs. Structural proteins, like keratin and collagen, build body parts.

prompt: The characteristics that you can see or measure, such as your height, make up your [[a]]. They are produced by your [[b]] and your environment working together.
hints: The second blank is the set of instructions you inherited from your parents.
solution: Your **phenotype** is the set of characteristics you show. It is produced by your **genes** and your environment together.

prompt: Which of these is an example of **discontinuous** variation in humans?

options.text: ABO blood group
Height
Body mass
Hand span

feedback.b: Height can be any value within a range, so it is continuous.
feedback.c: Body mass can be any value within a range, so it is continuous.
feedback.d: Hand span can be any value within a range, so it is continuous.

hints: Discontinuous variation falls into a few separate groups, with nothing in between.
solution: Everyone's blood group is A, B, AB or O, with nothing in between, so blood group shows **discontinuous** variation. The other three can be measured and take any value in a range.

prompt: Select **all** the examples of **continuous** variation.

options.text: Height
Body mass
Foot length
ABO blood group
Whether a pea seed is round or wrinkled

hints: Continuous variation can take any value in a range. Could you measure it with a ruler or scales?
solution: Height, body mass and foot length can be measured and take any value in a range, so they show **continuous** variation. Blood group and round or wrinkled pea seeds fall into separate groups, so they are **discontinuous**.

prompt: What is the scientific word for the passing of genetic information from parents to their offspring?
hints: It's the same word used when someone receives belongings left to them by a relative.
solution: **Inheritance** (or heredity) is the passing of genes from parents to their offspring.

prompt: Identical twins have exactly the same genes. One twin grows up with plenty of nutritious food, and the other has a poor diet. As adults, the first twin is 6 cm taller. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Their environment (diet) was different, and environment affects height as well as genes
The taller twin's genes changed because of the healthy food
Height is controlled only by the environment, not by genes
The taller twin inherited more height genes from their parents

feedback.b: Your genes don't change because of what you eat.
feedback.c: Genes affect height too. That's why tall parents often have tall children.
feedback.d: Identical twins have exactly the same genes, so this can't be the reason.

hints: If the genes are identical, what else is different?
solution: Identical twins have the same genes, so the difference must come from the **environment**. A good diet helps a person grow to the height their genes allow. Phenotype = genes + environment.

prompt: Which of these characteristics is caused **only** by the environment?

options.text: A scar from falling off a bike
ABO blood group
Natural eye colour
Height

feedback.b: Blood group is controlled by genes alone. Your environment can't change it.
feedback.c: Natural eye colour is controlled by genes.
feedback.d: Height depends on genes and on the environment, such as diet.

hints: Which one happened to the person during their life, rather than being in their genes?
solution: A scar is an **acquired** characteristic. It comes from something that happened during your life. It isn't in your genes, so you can't pass it on to your children.

prompt: Talia measures the hand span of 30 students in her class. Which type of graph should she use to show her results?

options.text: A histogram, because hand span is continuous data
A bar chart with gaps, because each student is a separate category
A pie chart, because it shows the whole class at once
A line graph, because hand span changes over time

feedback.b: Bar charts with gaps are for discontinuous data, such as blood groups. Hand span is measured, so it's continuous.
feedback.c: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. It isn't good for showing how measurements are spread across a range.
feedback.d: Talia measured each student once. Line graphs show how something changes over time.

hints: Is hand span continuous or discontinuous?
solution: Hand span can be any value in a range, so it is **continuous** data. Talia should group the measurements into classes (e.g. 16–17 cm, 17–18 cm) and draw a **histogram**, with the bars touching.

prompt: A dog's body cells each contain 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a dog's egg cell?
hints: Egg and sperm cells carry only one chromosome from each pair.
When an egg and a sperm join, the full number has to be restored.
solution:
Egg cells carry one chromosome from each pair, which is half the number: $78 \div 2 = 39$.

When a sperm (39) fertilises the egg (39), the puppy's cells get $39 + 39 = 78$ chromosomes.

prompt: Human body cells contain 23 [[a]] of chromosomes. In each pair, one chromosome came from the [[b]] and the other came from the father.
hints: 46 chromosomes is 23 groups of two.
You have two biological parents.
solution: Human body cells contain 23 **pairs** of chromosomes (46 in total). One chromosome of each pair came from the **mother** (in the egg) and the other from the father (in the sperm).

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: The chemical that carries genetic information
A long, coiled strand of DNA
A section of DNA that codes for one protein

hints: Start with the biggest structure: which one is a whole long strand?
solution: DNA → the chemical that carries genetic information. Chromosome → a long, coiled strand of DNA. Gene → a section of DNA that codes for one protein. Phenotype → the characteristics an organism shows.

prompt: Mia and her brother Leo have the same parents, but they look quite different. Why?

options.text: Each of them got a different mix of their parents' chromosomes
Mia got all her genes from her mother, and Leo got all his from their father
The older child always gets more of the parents' genes
Their genes keep changing as they grow, so they become different

feedback.b: Every child gets half their chromosomes from each parent.
feedback.c: Every child gets the same amount, half from each parent, whatever their age.
feedback.d: Your genes stay the same throughout your life.

hints: Each egg and each sperm carries half of a parent's chromosomes. Is it always the same half?
solution: Each egg and each sperm carries a random half of the parent's chromosomes, and every one is a different mix. So each child gets a **different combination** of their parents' genes. Only identical twins share the same combination.

prompt: Kai's dad is a professional rugby player who trains every day and is very fit. Kai says, "I'll be fit too, because I'll inherit Dad's fitness." Explain why Kai is only partly right.
modelAnswer: Kai inherits half his genes from his dad, so he may inherit some features that help in rugby, such as being tall or having a strong build. But fitness depends mostly on environment and lifestyle: how much you train, what you eat and how well you sleep. His dad became fit by training during his life. That is an acquired characteristic, which isn't stored in his DNA, so it can't be passed on. Kai will only be fit if he trains too.

rubric.criterion: States that genes from his dad may give Kai some helpful features (e.g. height or build)
States that fitness depends on environment or lifestyle, such as training and diet
Explains that characteristics acquired during life are not passed on in genes

hints: Which parts of being a good rugby player could come from genes?
How did Kai's dad become fit? Is that stored in his DNA?
solution: Genes might give Kai a helpful build, but fitness comes from training (environment). An acquired characteristic like fitness isn't in the DNA, so it can't be inherited.

prompt: Ruby takes cuttings from one hydrangea plant, so all the new plants have identical genes. She plants some in acidic soil and some in alkaline soil. The plants in acidic soil grow blue flowers, and the plants in alkaline soil grow pink flowers. What does this show?

options.text: The environment can change the phenotype, even when the genes are the same
The type of soil changed the plants' genes
The blue plants and pink plants are now different species
Flower colour is controlled only by genes

feedback.b: Soil doesn't change genes. The plants still have identical DNA.
feedback.c: They are still the same species. In fact, they are clones of the same plant.
feedback.d: If colour were controlled only by genes, identical plants would all have the same colour.

hints: The genes are identical. What is different?
solution: The plants are clones with identical genes, so the different flower colours must be caused by the **environment** (the soil). Phenotype = genes + environment.

prompt: Human height shows continuous variation. What is the best explanation for this?

options.text: Height is controlled by many genes and is also affected by the environment
Height is controlled by a single gene with two versions
Height is controlled only by the environment, such as diet
Height genes are only found in some of the body's cells

feedback.b: A single gene usually gives a few distinct groups (discontinuous variation), not a smooth range.
feedback.c: Genes affect height too. Tall parents tend to have tall children.
feedback.d: Almost every body cell contains the full set of genes.

hints: What usually controls a characteristic that falls into a few distinct groups?
Why would a smooth range of values appear?
solution: When **many genes** each add a little to a characteristic, and the **environment** (such as diet) also has an effect, the result is a smooth range of values: **continuous variation**. Single-gene characteristics usually give distinct groups instead.

prompt: Compare continuous and discontinuous variation. For each one, give an example and say which type of graph you would use to show it.
modelAnswer: Continuous variation can take any value within a range, for example height or hand span. It is usually controlled by many genes and is also affected by the environment. It is shown on a histogram, with the bars touching. Discontinuous variation falls into a few distinct groups, with nothing in between, for example ABO blood group. It is usually controlled by one gene (or a few), with little effect from the environment. It is shown on a bar chart with gaps between the bars.

rubric.criterion: Describes continuous variation as any value in a range, with a correct example
Describes discontinuous variation as distinct groups, with a correct example
States that continuous variation is usually many genes plus environment, and discontinuous is usually one (or a few) genes
Matches continuous data to a histogram and discontinuous data to a bar chart

hints: Describe what each type looks like, then give an example of each.
Think about whether the bars on the graph should touch.
solution:
| | Continuous | Discontinuous |
|---|---|---|
| Values | Any value in a range | A few distinct groups |
| Example | Height, hand span | ABO blood group |
| Usually caused by | Many genes + environment | One gene (or a few) |
| Graph | Histogram (bars touch) | Bar chart (gaps) |

prompt: Melanin is the pigment that colours skin, hair and eyes, and an enzyme is needed to make it. People with one type of albinism have faulty versions of the gene for this enzyme, so they have very pale skin and hair. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The faulty gene gives wrong instructions, so the enzyme doesn't work and very little melanin is made
Their skin cells have no DNA, so they can't make any proteins at all
Their skin cells have no nucleus, so melanin can't be stored there
Sunlight damaged their melanin gene sometime after they were born

feedback.b: Their cells do have DNA. Only one gene is faulty, so all their other proteins are made normally.
feedback.c: Skin cells do have a nucleus. The problem is the instructions in one gene.
feedback.d: Albinism is inherited: people are born with it. It isn't caused by sunlight.

hints: Think about the chain gene → protein → characteristic.
What happens to the characteristic if the protein can't do its job?
solution: A gene holds the instructions for making a protein, in this case an enzyme. If the instructions are faulty, the enzyme doesn't work, so very little melanin is made and the person has very pale skin and hair. This shows the chain **gene → protein → characteristic**.

prompt: Most bananas sold in shops are clones of one variety, called Cavendish, so they all have the same genes. Wild banana plants reproduce sexually. Explain why a new disease is a bigger threat to Cavendish bananas than to wild bananas.
modelAnswer: Because Cavendish bananas are clones, they all have identical genes. If a disease can infect one plant, it can infect all of them, because none has different genes that might protect it. The whole variety could be wiped out. Wild bananas reproduce sexually, so each plant gets a different mix of genes from its two parents. Because of this variation, some wild plants may have genes that help them resist the disease. Those plants survive and reproduce, passing on their genes, so the wild population carries on.

rubric.criterion: States that the clones all have identical genes, so a disease that affects one is likely to affect them all
States that sexual reproduction produces variation (offspring have different combinations of genes)
Explains that some of the varied wild plants may resist the disease and survive to reproduce

hints: What does it mean for the plants to be clones?
Why does variation matter when something in the environment changes?
solution: Identical clones would all be equally at risk. Sexual reproduction gives variation, so some wild plants may resist the disease, survive and pass on their genes.

prompt: What shape is a DNA molecule?

options.text: A double helix: two strands twisted around each other
A single straight strand, like a piece of string
Two separate straight strands lying side by side
A round ball made of tightly packed strands

feedback.b: DNA has two strands, and they are twisted, not straight.
feedback.c: The two strands of DNA are joined together and twisted into a spiral.
feedback.d: DNA is a very long, thin molecule. It coils up to form chromosomes, but its basic shape is a double helix.

hints: It is often compared to a twisted ladder.
solution: DNA is a **double helix**: two long strands twisted around each other, like a twisted ladder. The 'rungs' of the ladder carry the genetic code.

prompt: What do the letters **DNA** stand for?
hints: The 'N' and 'A' stand for two words that tell you it is an acid found in the nucleus.
solution: **DNA** stands for **deoxyribonucleic acid**. 'Nucleic' is because it is found in the nucleus, and 'deoxyribo' comes from the sugar (deoxyribose) in its strands.

prompt: Genes are sections of [[a]]. They are found on [[b]], which are inside the nucleus.
hints: Genes are made of the chemical that carries all genetic information.
These thread-like structures come in pairs in your body cells.
solution: Genes are sections of **DNA**. The DNA is coiled up into **chromosomes** inside the nucleus.

prompt: Which of these is an example of **discontinuous** variation in pea plants?

options.text: Flower colour (purple or white)
The length of the pea pods
The mass of each pea seed
The width of the leaves

feedback.b: Pod length can be any value within a range, so it shows continuous variation.
feedback.c: Seed mass can be any value within a range, so it shows continuous variation.
feedback.d: Leaf width can be any value within a range, so it shows continuous variation.

hints: Discontinuous variation falls into a few separate groups, with nothing in between.
solution: In discontinuous variation, there are a few distinct groups with nothing in between. Pea flowers are **either purple or white**. Pod length, seed mass and leaf width can be any value in a range, so they show continuous variation.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Passed on from parents in genes
Develops during an organism's life and isn't passed on in genes
Differences between individuals of the same species
The conditions around an organism, such as food, climate and lifestyle

hints: 'Acquired' means gained during life.
solution:
- **Inherited characteristic:** passed on from parents in genes (e.g. blood group).
- **Acquired characteristic:** develops during life and is not passed on (e.g. a scar).
- **Variation:** differences between individuals of the same species.
- **Environment:** the conditions around an organism.

prompt: What type of variation does leaf length show?

options.text: Continuous, because length can be any value within a range
Discontinuous, because the leaves were sorted into groups on the graph
Discontinuous, because every leaf has its own exact length
Continuous, because all of the leaves came from just one tree

feedback.b: Grouping the data into classes to draw the graph doesn't change the type of variation. Length can be any value, so it is continuous.
feedback.c: Lengths can be any value (5.2 cm, 5.25 cm and so on), not just a few fixed categories. That makes them continuous.
feedback.d: It is continuous, but not because the leaves came from one tree. It's continuous because length can be any value in a range.

hints: Could a leaf be 6.37 cm long? Or is length limited to a few set categories?
solution: Leaf length can take **any value within a range**, so it shows **continuous** variation. That is why it is shown on a histogram, with no gaps between the bars.

prompt: All the leaves came from the same tree, so they all have the same genes. Explain what must have caused the variation in their length.
modelAnswer: Because all the leaves have the same genes, the differences can't be caused by genes. They must be caused by the environment. For example, leaves in full sun and leaves in the shade grow differently, and leaves in different places on the tree get different amounts of water, nutrients and wind.

rubric.criterion: States that the leaves have identical genes, so the differences cannot be caused by genes
Explains that the environment causes the differences, with an example (e.g. light or shade, water, wind, position on the tree)

hints: If the genes are identical, what else can make leaves different?
Think about how conditions differ between the top, the bottom and the inside of a tree.
solution: Same genes means the variation must come from the **environment**: differences in light, water, nutrients and wind at different positions on the tree.

prompt: Select **all** the human characteristics that are affected by **both** genes and the environment.

options.text: Height
Body mass
Skin colour
ABO blood group
The language you speak (e.g. English or te reo Māori)
A scar from an injury

hints: For each one, ask: could your genes affect it? Could your diet, lifestyle or surroundings change it?
solution:
**Both:** height (genes plus diet and health), body mass (genes plus diet and exercise) and skin colour (genes plus time in the sun).

**Genes only:** ABO blood group.

**Environment only:** the language you speak, and a scar.

prompt: Put these stages in order to show how a baby gets its chromosomes.

items.text: A sperm (23 chromosomes) and an egg (23 chromosomes) are made
The fertilised egg divides again and again to make many cells
Every body cell in the baby has 46 chromosomes: 23 from each parent

hints: The sex cells must be made before they can meet.
Fertilisation happens before any of the cell divisions.
solution:
1. A sperm and an egg, each with 23 chromosomes, are made.
2. The sperm fertilises the egg.
3. The fertilised egg has $23 + 23 = 46$ chromosomes.
4. It divides over and over, copying the chromosomes each time.
5. So every body cell has the same 46 chromosomes, half from each parent.

prompt: What is the name for a permanent change in the DNA of a gene?
hints: These changes can happen randomly, or be caused by things such as UV light or radiation.
solution: A **mutation** is a change in DNA. Most mutations have no effect, some are harmful and a few are helpful. A mutation can change the protein that a gene codes for, which can change a characteristic. Mutations are the original source of new variation.

prompt: A characteristic that is controlled by **many** genes, and also affected by the environment, usually shows which pattern in a population?

options.text: A wide range of values, with most individuals near the middle
A few clear-cut groups, with nothing in between them
Every individual has exactly the same value
Most individuals are at the two extremes of the range

feedback.b: Clear-cut groups usually mean one gene (or very few), as with ABO blood groups. That's discontinuous variation.
feedback.c: Many genes plus the environment produce lots of variation, not identical individuals.
feedback.d: With many genes, most individuals get a mix of small effects that average out, so they end up near the middle, not at the extremes.

hints: Think about the shape of a histogram of human height.
solution: Each gene adds a small effect and the environment adds more, so the characteristic can be any value in a range: **continuous variation**. Most individuals are near the middle and few are at the extremes, giving a bell-shaped histogram, like the one for human height.

prompt:
Choose the type of protein for each example.

- Lipase, which breaks down fats in the small intestine: [[a]]
- Insulin, a chemical messenger made in the pancreas and carried in the blood: [[b]]
- Collagen, which makes skin, tendons and bones strong: [[c]]
hints: Enzymes speed up reactions. Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. Structural proteins build body parts.
solution: Lipase speeds up the breakdown of fats, so it is an **enzyme**. Insulin is a chemical messenger carried in the blood, so it is a **hormone**. Collagen builds strong body parts, so it is a **structural protein**.

stem:
Hōhepa follows these steps in a science lesson:

1. He mashes up a kiwifruit with salty water and a little dishwashing detergent.
2. He filters the mixture to remove the lumps.
3. He slowly pours ice-cold ethanol down the side of the tube, so that it forms a layer on top.
4. A white, stringy substance appears where the two layers meet.
prompt: The white, stringy substance came from the nuclei of the kiwifruit cells. What is it?
hints: It is the chemical that genes are made of.
solution: It is **DNA**. Millions of DNA molecules clump together in the cold ethanol, so you can see them as white threads, even though a single DNA molecule is far too thin to see.

stem:
Hōhepa follows these steps in a science lesson:

1. He mashes up a kiwifruit with salty water and a little dishwashing detergent.
2. He filters the mixture to remove the lumps.
3. He slowly pours ice-cold ethanol down the side of the tube, so that it forms a layer on top.
4. A white, stringy substance appears where the two layers meet.
prompt: Why did Hōhepa add dishwashing detergent?

options.text: To break down the membranes around the cells and nuclei, releasing the DNA
To clean the DNA, so that it shows up as white instead of green
To make the DNA dissolve completely in the cold ethanol layer
To break down the cell walls, so that the cells shrink and die

feedback.b: The detergent isn't for cleaning. DNA looks white when lots of it clumps together.
feedback.c: DNA does **not** dissolve in cold ethanol. That is why it appears as a solid where the layers meet.
feedback.d: Mashing breaks up the cell walls. The detergent breaks down the membranes, which are made of fat-like substances.

hints: Think about what dishwashing liquid does to grease on a plate.
Cell membranes are made partly of fat-like substances (lipids).
solution: The cell membrane and the membrane around the nucleus are made of fat-like substances (lipids). Detergent breaks them apart, just as it breaks up grease, so the **DNA is released** from the nucleus into the liquid.

stem:
Hōhepa follows these steps in a science lesson:

1. He mashes up a kiwifruit with salty water and a little dishwashing detergent.
2. He filters the mixture to remove the lumps.
3. He slowly pours ice-cold ethanol down the side of the tube, so that it forms a layer on top.
4. A white, stringy substance appears where the two layers meet.
prompt: Explain how the DNA that Hōhepa extracted is related to chromosomes, genes and proteins in the kiwifruit cells.
modelAnswer: In each kiwifruit cell, the DNA is in the nucleus, coiled up tightly to form chromosomes. A gene is a section of the DNA on a chromosome. Each gene carries the instructions (the code) for making one protein. The proteins then produce the fruit's characteristics: for example, enzymes make the sugars that give the fruit its sweet taste.

rubric.criterion: States that the DNA is coiled up to form chromosomes, in the nucleus
States that a gene is a section of DNA (on a chromosome)
Explains that a gene carries the instructions (code) for making a protein, which affects a characteristic

hints: Start with the largest structure (a chromosome) and work down to the smallest (a gene).
What does a gene carry the instructions to make?
solution: DNA → coiled into **chromosomes** in the nucleus. A **gene** is a section of that DNA. Each gene is the code for one **protein**, and proteins (such as enzymes) produce the characteristics of the fruit.

prompt: Mere's dog lost the tip of its tail in an accident. Mere thinks the dog's puppies will be born with short tails. Explain whether she is right, using the ideas of inherited and acquired characteristics.
modelAnswer: Mere is wrong. The short tail is an acquired characteristic: it was caused by an accident during the dog's life, not by its genes. The accident didn't change the DNA in the dog's sperm or egg cells. The puppies inherit genes, not injuries, and the genes still carry the instructions for a normal tail, so the puppies will be born with normal tails.

rubric.criterion: States that the short tail is an acquired characteristic (caused by the environment/an accident during its life)
States that an injury doesn't change the genes (DNA) in the dog's sex cells
Concludes that the puppies inherit genes for a normal tail, so they will have normal tails

hints: Was the short tail caused by genes or by something that happened during its life?
What do the puppies actually inherit from their parents?
solution: **Acquired characteristics aren't inherited.** Only genes are passed on, through sperm and egg cells. Losing part of a tail doesn't change the dog's genes, so the puppies will have normal tails.

stem: Romney sheep are farmed all over New Zealand. Each body cell of a sheep contains 54 chromosomes, in 27 pairs. A Romney ram (male) and a Romney ewe (female) are mated, and the ewe gives birth to a lamb.
prompt: How many chromosomes are in each of the ram's sperm cells?
hints: Sex cells (sperm and eggs) carry half the normal number of chromosomes.
They carry one chromosome from each pair.
solution: A sperm cell carries one chromosome from each pair: $54 \div 2 = 27$ chromosomes.

stem: Romney sheep are farmed all over New Zealand. Each body cell of a sheep contains 54 chromosomes, in 27 pairs. A Romney ram (male) and a Romney ewe (female) are mated, and the ewe gives birth to a lamb.
prompt: Why must sperm and egg cells contain only half the normal number of chromosomes?

options.text: So that when they join at fertilisation, the lamb has the normal number (54)
So that they are small and light enough to move around easily
So that the lamb inherits genes from only one of its two parents
Because sex cells only need the genes for the lamb's appearance

feedback.b: Halving the chromosomes isn't about size. Egg cells are actually some of the largest cells.
feedback.c: The lamb inherits genes from **both** parents: half from the ram and half from the ewe.
feedback.d: Each sex cell carries a full set of genes for all of the lamb's characteristics: one chromosome from every pair.

hints: What happens to the number of chromosomes when a sperm and an egg join?
solution: At fertilisation, a sperm (27 chromosomes) joins an egg (27 chromosomes), giving $27 + 27 = 54$, the normal number for a sheep. If sex cells had 54 each, the number would double in every generation.

stem: Romney sheep are farmed all over New Zealand. Each body cell of a sheep contains 54 chromosomes, in 27 pairs. A Romney ram (male) and a Romney ewe (female) are mated, and the ewe gives birth to a lamb.
prompt: The farmer wants future lambs to grow heavier fleeces (more wool). Explain how she could use selective breeding to do this over several generations.
modelAnswer: She should choose the ram and the ewes with the heaviest fleeces and breed only from them. Fleece weight is partly controlled by genes, and lambs inherit genes from both parents, so these lambs are more likely to have heavy fleeces too. From the lambs, she again chooses the ones with the heaviest fleeces to breed, and repeats this every generation. Over many generations, more of the flock will carry the genes for heavy fleeces. She should feed all the sheep in the same way, so that she is choosing sheep for their genes, not just because they were better fed.

rubric.criterion: Chooses parents with the wanted characteristic (the heaviest fleeces) to breed
Explains that the offspring inherit genes from both parents, so they are more likely to have heavy fleeces
Repeats the selection with the best offspring over many generations

hints: Which sheep should she allow to breed?
One generation isn't enough. What should she do with the lambs?
solution: **Selective breeding:** choose the best parents → breed them → choose the best offspring → breed them → repeat for many generations. Because the characteristic is partly controlled by genes, it becomes more common in the flock over time.

prompt: Dogs have 78 chromosomes in each body cell, humans have 46, and potato plants have 48. Hemi says this means dogs are more complex than humans. Which response is best?

options.text: No. Chromosome number doesn't show how complex an organism is: potatoes have more than humans.
Yes. More chromosomes always means more genes, so it means a more complex organism.
No. Humans must have more chromosomes than dogs, because humans are more complex.
Yes. Dogs have more chromosomes in each cell because they have more cells in their body.

feedback.b: Chromosome number does not match complexity: a potato plant has more chromosomes than a human. What matters is the genes the DNA carries, not how many pieces it is divided into.
feedback.c: The data shows that humans have **fewer** chromosomes (46) than dogs (78).
feedback.d: Every body cell of an organism has the same number of chromosomes, however many cells the organism has.

hints: Compare the potato with the human.
solution: The number of chromosomes varies between species, but it doesn't show complexity: potato plants (48) have more than humans (46), and dogs (78) have more still. What matters is the genes the DNA carries.

prompt: In humans, the sex chromosomes are usually XX in females and XY in males. Which sex cell decides whether a baby has XX or XY sex chromosomes?

options.text: The sperm, because each sperm carries either an X or a Y chromosome
The egg, because each egg carries either an X or a Y chromosome
Both equally, because each parent passes on one sex chromosome
Neither: the temperature that the baby develops at decides it

feedback.b: Every egg carries an X chromosome, because females are XX.
feedback.c: Each parent does pass on one sex chromosome, but the egg always gives an X. Only the sperm can give either X or Y, so the sperm decides.
feedback.d: Temperature decides sex in tuatara and some other reptiles, but not in humans.

hints: Which sex chromosomes can a female (XX) pass on? Which can a male (XY) pass on?
solution: Every egg carries an **X**. About half of sperm carry an X and half carry a Y. If an X sperm fertilises the egg, the baby is XX; if a Y sperm does, the baby is XY. So the **sperm** decides.

prompt: A skin cell and a muscle cell from the same person contain exactly the same genes, but they look different and do different jobs. Explain how this is possible. (Use the idea that a gene can be 'switched on', so the cell uses it, or 'switched off'.)
modelAnswer: All of the body's cells come from one fertilised egg, and the DNA is copied each time a cell divides, so every body cell has the same genes. But not every gene is used in every cell. In a muscle cell, the genes for the proteins that let it contract are switched on. In a skin cell, other genes are switched on instead, such as the gene for keratin. Different genes switched on means different proteins are made, so the cells end up with different structures and do different jobs.

rubric.criterion: Explains that all body cells come from one fertilised egg (with DNA copied at each division), so they have the same genes
States that different genes are switched on (used) in different types of cell
Links this to different proteins being made, giving each type of cell a different structure and job

hints: Every body cell came from the same fertilised egg.
Does every cell have to use every gene it carries?
solution: Same genes, but **different genes are switched on** in different cells. Each type of cell makes only the proteins it needs, so cells **specialise**.

prompt: Scientists take the nucleus out of a body cell from a **black** sheep. They put it into an egg cell from a **white** sheep, after removing the egg's own nucleus. The egg grows into an embryo, which is placed inside a third, **white** sheep, and she gives birth to the lamb. What colour will the lamb's wool be?

options.text: Black, because its genes came from the black sheep's nucleus
White, because its egg cell came from a white sheep
White, because the sheep that gave birth to it is white
Grey, because it gets a mix of genes from black and white sheep

feedback.b: The egg's own nucleus was removed, so the egg gave the lamb no genes for wool colour.
feedback.c: The sheep that gave birth gave the lamb somewhere to grow, and food, but none of its genes.
feedback.d: All of the lamb's chromosomes came from one nucleus, so its genes match the black sheep. They are not a mix.

hints: Which part of a cell contains the chromosomes?
Which sheep did that part come from?
solution: The nucleus contains the chromosomes, and therefore the genes. The lamb's nucleus came from the black sheep, so it has the black sheep's genes and will have **black** wool. This is how Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996: she looked like the sheep that gave the nucleus, not like the egg donor or the sheep that gave birth to her.

prompt: Discuss the statement: "Your genes decide everything about you." Use examples in your answer.
modelAnswer: The statement is only partly true. Genes carry the instructions for making proteins, so some characteristics are controlled by genes alone: for example, your ABO blood group is set by your genes and can't be changed by your lifestyle. Many characteristics are affected by both genes and the environment: your genes set a range for your height, but your diet and health while you are growing decide where you end up in that range. Body mass, and skin colour (with tanning), are similar. Some characteristics come only from the environment, such as the language you speak, a scar, or a skill you have learned. So your characteristics (your phenotype) come from your genes and your environment working together.

rubric.criterion: Gives an example of a characteristic controlled by genes alone (e.g. ABO blood group)
Gives an example of a characteristic affected by both genes and environment, and explains how (e.g. height: genes plus diet)
Gives an example of a characteristic caused only by the environment (e.g. a scar, the language you speak, a learned skill)
Concludes that the statement is only partly true, because characteristics (phenotype) come from genes and the environment together

hints: Sort characteristics into three groups: genes only, environment only, and both.
Finish with a clear conclusion: is the statement true, false or partly true?
solution: A strong answer gives examples of all three kinds of characteristic (**genes only**, **both**, **environment only**) and concludes that **phenotype = genes + environment**, so the statement is only partly true.
